title:
PIXEL TRAIL:
BASE CAMP
subtitle: Daily briefings for Lessons 1 to 5
tagline: Make games in p5.js, one step at a time.

lessons.title: Hello, Canvas

board.lesson: Hello, Canvas. Tell the computer exactly where to put dots, and draw your first scene.
board.question: Why does a computer need such exact instructions, when a person could guess what you mean?
board.agenda:
1. Meet the grid
2. See how a line of code is built
3. Draw a sun and the ground
4. Add color
5. Build your own character
board.riddle: Every dot on your screen has an address on me. I count across from the left and down from the top. What am I?

vocab: The area your program draws on.
Two numbers, (x, y), that say where something is. x counts from the left. y counts down from the top.
A command: a name, then values in parentheses, like ellipse(340, 60, 70, 70);
A value you give a command, placed inside the parentheses.
standards: 6-8.CT.d.6: Use an iterative approach in development and debugging to understand the dimensions of a problem clearly.
lessons.main: Build a character out of at least three shapes, standing on the ground.
stretch: Add a cloud made of three overlapping ellipses.
Use triangle to draw a mountain behind your character.
Add a house or a tree to the scene.

lessons.title: It Moves!

board.lesson: It Moves! Give the computer a memory, and your scene comes alive.
board.question: How does a program remember something that keeps changing?
board.agenda:
1. See how draw() repeats
2. Create a variable
3. Use it to place the saucer
4. Change it every frame
5. Add a second moving thing
board.riddle: I have a name, and I hold one thing at a time. Give me something new and I forget the old. What am I?

vocab: A named box that holds a value. The value can change.
The word that makes a new variable, like let saucerX = 50;
draw() runs again and again, about 60 times every second.
One picture in an animation. A game is a very fast flipbook.
standards: 6-8.CT.b.2: Use logical reasoning to predict outputs given varying inputs.
6-8.CT.d.4: Implement problem solutions using a programming language, including all of the following: looping behavior, conditional statements, expressions, variables, and functions.
lessons.main: Add a second variable of your own that moves something else.
stretch: Make something grow by putting a variable in the width of an ellipse.
Make the background slowly change color using a variable.
Add a third variable for the saucer's speed.

lessons.title: Puppet Master

board.lesson: Puppet Master. Your program starts listening, and you build a creature that follows you around.
board.question: How can a program respond to the person using it?
board.agenda:
1. Follow the mouse
2. Do math inside your code
3. Write your first if
4. Show a number on screen
5. Make your creature your own
board.riddle: I am small, I have a tail, and I never eat cheese. Your program always knows where I am. What am I?

vocab: Information going into a program, like where the mouse is.
Variables p5 keeps updated with the mouse's position.
Math the computer works out for you, like mouseX + 20.
Code that runs only when its condition is true.
standards: 6-8.CT.b.2: Use logical reasoning to predict outputs given varying inputs.
6-8.CT.d.4: Implement problem solutions using a programming language, including all of the following: looping behavior, conditional statements, expressions, variables, and functions.
lessons.main: Make something new respond to the mouse.
stretch: Make the pupils look toward the mouse.
Add a hat that only appears when the mouse is on the right half of the canvas.
Use pmouseX to draw a trail.

lessons.title: Bounce House

board.lesson: Bounce House. Your objects learn about walls, and your code starts making decisions.
board.question: How do programs make decisions?
board.agenda:
1. Spot the problem
2. Bounce off all four walls
3. Fix the sinking edge
4. Change color and count bounces
5. Bug hunt
board.riddle: I am a tiny word that asks a question. When the answer is no, I skip everything inside me. What am I?

vocab: A question with a true or false answer, like ballX > width.
Code that runs only when its condition is true.
Checking two values with > (greater than) or < (less than).
An edge your code has to check, like a wall of the canvas.
standards: 6-8.CT.b.5: Recognize that boundaries need to be taken into account for an algorithm to produce correct results.
6-8.CT.d.6: Use an iterative approach in development and debugging to understand the dimensions of a problem clearly.
6-8.CT.b.1: Design solutions that use repetition and conditionals.
6-8.CT.b.2: Use logical reasoning to predict outputs given varying inputs.
lessons.main: Write the wall checks yourself, then find and fix the bug.
stretch: Speed the ball up a little on every bounce.
Add a second ball with its own four variables.
Make the ball bounce off a paddle at your mouse.

lessons.title: Catch the Star

board.lesson: Catch the Star. Your first real game, with a player, a goal, a score, and a way to lose.
board.question: What turns a drawing into a game?
board.agenda:
1. Keep the stars falling
2. Add a score
3. Catch the star
4. Add lives and a game over
5. Make it get harder
board.riddle: Ask me the same question twice and you may get two different answers, yet I am never wrong. What am I?

vocab: Collision detection is checking whether two things are touching.
Only one part has to be true.
random(a, b) gives a surprise number between a and b.
standards: 6-8.CT.b.1: Design solutions that use repetition and conditionals.
6-8.CT.b.3: Individually and collaboratively decompose a problem and create a sub-solution for each of its parts (e.g., video game, robot obstacle course, making dinner).
6-8.CT.d.4: Implement problem solutions using a programming language, including all of the following: looping behavior, conditional statements, expressions, variables, and functions.
6-8.CT.d.6: Use an iterative approach in development and debugging to understand the dimensions of a problem clearly.
lessons.main: Make your game get harder as the player improves, and make it your own.
stretch: Add a bad star, in a different color, that costs a life when you catch it.
Keep and show a best score.
